To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the following factors may cause accelerated decomposition: 1) exposure to high temperatures, both indoor and outdoor; 2) exposure to central heating; 3) exposure to hot water; 4) exposure to electric blankets; 5) exposure to saunas; 6) exposure to motor vehicles; 7) fever; 8) infections; 9) illicit and prescription drugs; 10) obesity; 11) insulin-dependent diabetes mellitis.

the following factors and processes may cause accelerated decomposition in human bodies: exposure to elevated environmental temperature, both outdoors and indoor; exposure to increased humidity; fires; exposure to central heating; hot water; saunas; electric blankets; deaths within motor vehicles; and fever, infections, insulin-dependent diabetes, and obesity.
there are several factors that can accelerate putrefaction, and that the putrefactive changes are more advanced when these factors are present.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the processes and factors that influence decomposition and how these factors can influence the rate of decomposition.
the identification and characterization of factors and processes that may lead to the accelerated decomposition of cadavers.
the study of decomposition of human cadavers and the factors and processes causing accelerated putrefaction and autolysis in human cadavers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the body was found in a state of advanced decomposition, and this may be attributed to a combination of exogenous and/or endogenous factors.
the body is in the early stages of decomposition, which is consistent with the circumstances of death.
decomposition was accelerated, but that the time since death was still consistent with that given by the witness statement or the time of death.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the decomposition of a body is not only a function of time but also of many other factors.
in the case of the human body, the rate of putrefaction is not constant, but rather, varies with the environment in which the cadaver is found.
there are a number of external factors which may enhance decomposition and a number of endogenous factors that may accelerate putrefactive processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are many factors that may cause accelerated decomposition in human bodies and these need to be considered in any case where decomposition has occurred.
there are many factors which can influence decomposition.

the forensic pathologist should be alert to the possibility that the decomposition process may be accelerated by external or internal factors and that the pathologist should be aware that these factors may be responsible for artefactual changes in the body.
